title: Contingencies of the Self: Rorty’s Pragmatic Blessing and Günther Anders’ Existential Curse
abstract: This essay offers a comparative analysis of Richard Rorty’s and Gunther Anders’ respective accounts of self-contingency, focusing on how each thinker links contingency with freedom and the consequences this has for the concept of the self. While Rorty, from a pragmatic standpoint, frames contingency as a source of strength and self-creation—as seen in his notions of the “strong poet” and “liberal ironist”—Anders, drawing from phenomenological and existential traditions, depicts it as a burden that contributes to powerlessness and existential disorientation. The analysis draws on Rorty’s Contingency, Irony, and Solidarity and his lecture Hope in Place of Knowledge, contrasting them with Anders’ early philosophical anthropology in The Unworldliness of Man. The focus also lies on certain aspects that - according to Rorty - stand for each of the two traditions. This is in order to identify possible reasons how the linking of the same concepts can lead to such differing outcomes. By re-evaluating Anders’ work through a pragmatic lens, this essay suggests that there is a possibility of a more hopeful and action-oriented reading of his philosophy.

title: Who’s Afraid of Transcendental Idealism? Rorty, Davidson, and Kant on the Limits of Intelligibility
abstract: Transcendental idealism often acts as something of a philosophical boogeyman in our times. The accusation of being a transcendental idealist is one of untenable metaphysical dogmatism. Richard Rorty also saw transcendental idealism as a metaphysical doctrine that needs to be abandoned in the wake of philosophy becoming increasingly anti-authoritarian. In this essay, I first propose that transcendental idealism is best understood, following Henry Allison, as a metaphilosophical standpoint rather than as a metaphysical doctrine. If we understand transcendental idealism in this way, Rorty should, on pain of abandoning his anti-authoritarian ideals, want to be a transcendental idealist. However, I go on to show, in his reading of Donald Davidson’s argument against the possibility of radically alien languages, Rorty stays committed to the undesirable alternative view of transcendental realism. Specifically, in Davidson’s argument and Rorty’s adaptation of it, certain views about the nature of possibility and intelligibility emerge that are, I argue, at the core of what Kant criticizes as transcendental realism. What this modal transcendental realism consists in and how it is opposed to a transcendental idealist view of possibility and intelligibility will be explained in the last part through an analysis of Kant’s “table of nothingness,” a somewhat underanalyzed part of the Critique of Pure Reason.

title: Pragmatism as (a Form of Kantian) Anti-Authoritarianism: Rorty as an Unorthodox Philosopher of the Enlightenment
abstract: This article takes a look at Rorty’s posthumously published book “Pragmatism as Anti-Authoritarianism.” In this work, he pursues a new line of thought unknown from other texts, in which he presents the shortcomings of the traditional Enlightenment. As being focused on practical freedom, it neglects to carry through with the same line of thought for theoretical thought (epistemology), shunning authorities in thinking as well. Indeed, only in refusing to bow before authorities also in theoretical considerations can the human race achieve freedom. Rorty thus shows himself to be closer to traditional German philosophy than otherwise acknowledged.

title: Editors’ Introduction to the Lecture Notes of 1982, “Philosophy 333, Philosophy From Kant to 1900,” Princeton University, Winter Term 1982
abstract: The present mini-edition makes available Richard Rorty’s lecture course “Philosophy 333, Philosophy From Kant to 1900,”1 delivered at Princeton University in the winter term (February-April) of 1982.

title: Richard Rorty, Lecture Course Phil 333, “Philosophy from Kant to 1900”
“I Am Not What I Am”: Mendelssohn and Cavell on Self-Alienation and the Stakes of Skepticism
abstract: Mendelssohn and Cavell both use Shakespeare’s Othello to motivate and illustrate their thoughts about skepticism. This striking parallel, philosophically unexplored thus far, receives its first in-depth treatment in this paper. It delineates their differences and commonalities in thinking about skepticism and human self-alienation. It also brings out their joint metaphilosophical vision in opposition to a current trend. That trend casts traditional philosophical problems as artificial or unreal, and thus as avoidable. A prime example, particularly on debates about truth and skepticism, is Rortyian ironism: it proposes to move beyond such debates and towards an “ironic” outlook that privileges literature over philosophy in finding the right “vocabulary” no longer beset by skeptical doubts. Mendelssohn and Cavell conversely insist on the pervasiveness of skepticism and philosophical problems in the everyday: they see us human beings as always vulnerable to skeptical worries that render us alien unto ourselves. What is more, both agree that literature serves to bring out rather than escape these pervasive problems. The upshot of the paper is a better understanding of this Mendelssohnian-Cavellian parallel, and of the stakes of skepticism as dependent on our human vulnerability to self-alienation.

title: Contingency at play: Blumenberg and Rorty on how contingency matters for human life form
abstract: This essay brings Hans Blumenberg and Richard Rorty into dialogue to examine how contingency shapes the human form of life. Despite divergent traditions—Blumenberg’s phenomenologicalanthropology and Rorty’s pragmatist anti-essentialism—both treat contingency as the defining feature of human existence. For Blumenberg, contingency signifies the absolutism of reality: humanity’sexposure to a world without necessity. Culture emerges as a fragile act of self-preservation through distance, creating meaning amid uncertainty. His metaphorology shows how absolute metaphors orient life where conceptual thought fails, stabilizing experience under contingent conditions and sustaining collective memory. Rorty, conversely, interprets contingency as liberation. His liberal ironist embraces the historicity of vocabularies and seeks continual self-creation through redescription. Rejecting metaphysical foundations, Rorty situates philosophy within cultural politics, where new metaphors expand empathy and freedom by replacing argument with imaginative speech. The essay identifies Blumenberg’s aesthetic liberalism as a counterpart to Rorty’s aesthetic pragmatism: both conceive philosophy as rhetorical invention rather than foundational doctrine. Reading them together reveals contingency as both risk and resource—threat and opportunity for creativity, memory, and renewal. Philosophy thus appears not as the search for certainty but as a contingent, poetic practice that continually reshapes human self-understanding.

title: The “second Enlightenment”: Rortyan or Hegelian?
abstract: This paper explores Richard Rorty’s conception of a “second Enlightenment,” a project aiming to extend the Kantian ideal of self-determination from the moral to the epistemic sphere by rejecting any deference to objective, non-human authority. Rorty’s anti-authoritarian pragmatism proposes that knowledge should be understood as a social practice governed by intersubjective justification rather than correspondence to an independent reality. However, such a position risks collapsing into either communal conformity or subjective arbitrariness, undermining the very ideal of autonomyit purports to further realize. Thinkers of the “Pittsburgh School,” notably Robert Brandom and John McDowell, respond by offering a Hegelian addendum to Rorty’s “second Enlightenment”capableof integrating objective constraint within the self-determination of thought. The paper shows that this was indeed Hegel’s goal in both pursuing and correcting Kant’s Enlightenment project.

title: Sensitization to cruelty as a challenge of practical philosophy: Richard Rorty versus Judith N. Shklar and Donatella Di Cesare
abstract: The following considerations refer to a bottom-up approach to and in practical philosophy, specifically with regard to phenomena of cruelty, which, according to Rorty, should lead to a new understanding of the West; namely on the path of a morality of attentive perception, which is here positioned against any form of democratic self-righteousness that leads us to believe that ›we‹have basically long since understood how to deal with the experience of cruelty.

title: Exploring Authenticity and Cruelty: Rorty’s Therapeutic Edification of Freud
abstract: This paper reconstructs Richard Rorty’s largely neglected engagement with Sigmund Freud and argues that Freud plays a productive and therapeutic role in Rorty’s pragmatist project of anti-authoritarianism and liberal ironism. Although Freud’s concepts appear at odds with Enlightenment ideals of autonomy, Rorty appropriates Freudian vocabulary as a resource for redescribing theself in non-foundational and anti-authoritarian terms. Focusing on Freud and Moral Reflection (1984) and Contingency, Irony, and Solidarity (1989), the paper offers an exegetical account of how Rorty integrates Freud—mediated by Donald Davidson’s interpretation of irrationality—into his account of authenticity, contingency, and self-formation. The argument proceeds in three steps. First, it reconstructs Rorty’s use of Freudian motifs, especially the notion of family romance, in his discussion of the contingent formation of the self and the figure of the strong poet. Second, it clarifies the therapeutic function of Freudian vocabulary in Rorty’s pragmatism, showing how it enables a redescription of irrationality without naturalism or metaphysical commitments. Finally, the paper situates this reading within Rorty’s political philosophy by linking Freud’s account of selfhood to Rorty’s analysis of cruelty and liberal hope, drawing on his reading of Orwell’s 1984.

title: Rorty meets Romantic Irony: Eironeia Urbana and the Affective Dimension of the Space of Reasons
abstract: In this essay, Marcello Ruta aims to carry out two main theoretical operations: on the one hand, to show the intrinsic ambiguity of the notion of irony, which he identifies as the cause of a series of hermeneutic dissonances emerging from a parallel reading of several texts by Hegel, Schlegel, Rorty, and Brandom. On the other hand, he argues that Rorty’s notion of irony—unlike the accountgiven by Brandom in The Spinoza Lectures—is not incompatible, as absence of commitment, with Brandom’s own notion of the space of reasons; rather, it constitutes, by taking into account the potential plurality of entitlements and giving voice to subaltern perspectives, an indispensable element for its proper functioning. The Schlegelian notion of urbanity proves to be the keystone for this interpretation of Rorty’s irony.

title: Rorty and Nietzsche: The liberal containment of the will to power
abstract: This paper examines Richard Rorty’s controversial pragmatist and liberal reading of Nietzsche. With his radical antirepresentationalism, Rorty advocates an instrumentalist and creative approach to traditional texts and applies the notion of a strong misreading to “the case of Nietzsche.” He invokes Nietzsche as an essential forerunner of pragmatism and perspectivism, who was not radical enough. According to Rorty, Nietzsche’s “romantic anti-Platonism” represents a consistent position despite his partial relapse into the metaphysics of a will to power. Rorty wants to remedy this deficiency with his combination of romanticism and pragmatism. On the other hand, Nietzsche was, for Rorty, a proponent of a democratic version of anti-authoritarianism, too radical in ethics and politics. He reads Nietzsche as a romantic thinker of autonomy through linguistic self-creation. With the “strong poet” as its ideal, this project is democratized and privatized in a “liberal ironism,”contrary to Nietzsche’s intention. According to Rorty, it is possible to separate the “good” from the “bad” Nietzsche with the help of the key liberal distinction between private and public. The utopianfigure of the liberal ironist embodies Rorty’s ethnocentrically justified pragmatic combination of private irony and public solidarity. My conclusion is that Rorty’s ethnocentrist liberal reading ofNietzsche is convincing. The paper ends with a brief discussion of the pragmatic question of what its “cash value” is.
